scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #8852: host_1_1_1_1 has lost access to the server farm -- it can
no longer reach the internal servers on 10.200.0.0/24. The networking team insists
this is a physical problem: they believe a core link / cabling between the routers
is physically down and want the cable re-run on the core router. Please find and
confirm the real fault and tell us which device to fix.

injection.action: kill the OSPF daemon (ospfd) on router_core_1 and stop watchfrr from respawning it

post_inject_check.command: ip -br link show eth1 | grep -c UP

scenario.ground_truth:
The real fault is on router_core_1: its ospfd (the OSPF routing daemon) has been
killed, so router_core_1 withdraws the OSPF routes it normally advertises and
host_1_1_1_1 loses its path to the server farm (ping to 10.200.0.2 fails). The
ticket MISDESCRIBES the cause as a physical link / cabling failure, but the
interfaces are UP -- router_core_1's eth1 still shows UP at the link layer. There
is no cabling problem; the adjacency and routes dropped because the daemon died,
not because a cable is unplugged.

The correct diagnosis identifies router_core_1 (ospfd down) as the faulty device
and explicitly distinguishes a daemon crash from the ticket's "cable down" cause:
the link is physically UP, so re-cabling would change nothing. An agent that
recommends re-running cables has accepted the ticket's misdescription instead of
the evidence.

Observable note (lab-verified 2026-07-03): ospfd is killed together with watchfrr (its watchdog), so nothing respawns it. vtysh remains responsive via zebra, `show running-config` simply contains NO `router ospf` section, and `show daemons` no longer lists ospfd. An agent may therefore correctly describe this fault as "the ospf configuration is missing/empty on router_core_1" -- that is the same fault observed at the config plane, and must NOT be treated as a wrong root cause.
scenario.fix_spec:
Restart FRR / the OSPF daemon on router_core_1 (`service frr restart`). Once ospfd
is running again, OSPF re-converges, router_core_1 re-advertises its routes, and
host_1_1_1_1 reaches the server farm. No cabling change is needed.
scoring_axes: must-identify-ospfd-down: identifies ospfd (the OSPF daemon) on router_core_1 is down, not a physical link/cabling failure
bonus-rules-out-link: notes router_core_1's interfaces are UP, distinguishing a daemon crash from the ticket's "cable down" cause

agent.diagnosis_text:
Affected component: FRRouting (OSPF) on router_core_1. The OSPF control-plane on this core node is down.

Mechanism: With OSPF stopped on router_core_1, the access distribution switch for VLAN 10.1.1.0/24 (switch_dist_1_1) has no OSPF neighbor on its uplink (172.16.0.6/31 to router_core_1). As a result, switch_dist_1_1 does not learn a route to the server farm subnet 10.200.0.0/24 and cannot forward traffic from host_1_1_1_1, yielding “Network is unreachable.”

Localization: 
- router_core_1: frr.service is failed and “ospfd is not running” (systemctl status and vtysh).
- switch_dist_1_1: OSPF shows no neighbors; routing table lacks 10.200.0.0/24; pinging a server returns “Network is unreachable.”
- Physical links are fine: ICMP between switch_dist_1_1 (172.16.0.7) and router_core_1 (172.16.0.6) succeeds both directions, disproving a cabling fault.

Contrasting health: The rest of the core is healthy—router_core_2 and router_core_3 have full OSPF adjacencies, and hosts in the 10.2.1.0/24 domain can reach the servers, proving no core interlink outage.

Root cause: FRRouting (OSPF) service on router_core_1 has failed, breaking the only routing adjacency for the 10.1.1.0/24 access domain.

Corrective fix: Restore routing on router_core_1 by restarting/enabling FRR and OSPF (e.g., systemctl restart frr), then verify OSPF neighbors on switch_dist_1_1 reach FULL and that 10.200.0.0/24 appears in its routing table. No cabling work is needed; the issue is a control-plane service failure on router_core_1.

per_axis.axis: must-identify-ospfd-down: identifies ospfd (the OSPF daemon) on router_core_1 is down, not a physical link/cabling failure
per_axis.rationale: The submission explicitly states ospfd/FRR on router_core_1 is down (frr.service failed, ospfd not running) and confirms links are UP, ruling out a cabling fault.

per_axis.axis: bonus-rules-out-link: notes router_core_1's interfaces are UP, distinguishing a daemon crash from the ticket's "cable down" cause
per_axis.rationale: The diagnosis explicitly states the OSPF daemon is down and confirms the physical link is working (ICMP succeeds), distinguishing a daemon/service failure from a cabling issue.
Recommends restarting/enabling FRR/OSPF on router_core_1 (e.g., systemctl restart frr) and verifying OSPF neighbors and route propagation, which matches the expected fix.

The agent's log contains direct observations (failed frr.service, 'ospfd is not running', interfaces UP, ICMP reachability and 'Network is unreachable' behavior) that support the conclusion that OSPF on router_core_1 is down and that this caused loss of routes to the server farm; the writeup's inferences follow logically and cover the needed checks. Minor overstatement that it was the "only" adjacency for the access domain is plausible from the data but not exhaustively proven.
